<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
I've read it carefully. This is a strong, responsive follow-up. It takes up the open questions from all three earlier papers:
- **Hours:** log-in time is added as a second hours measure.
- **Mechanism:** meetings are tested under a registered mediation analysis.
- **Durability:** the trial is extended to 24 months.

It also finds the fact that settles the meta-analysis's decay claim: all four long studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which is what I suspected in my last review. The arithmetic checks out:
- 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8%, and 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5%.
- Halden: 34.9/40.3 is −13.4%, and 96.8/86.6 is +11.8%.
- The mediation shares sum to 100%.

The remaining problems are below, most important first. One of them changes how the decline should be read.

## 1. The control offices' meeting audit contaminates the decline estimate

Two of the seven control offices cut meetings in month 15 and raised their output per hour by 4.1%. The paper presents this as evidence that reorganisation alone might capture some of the gain. But it is also **contamination of the comparison group**, and it biases the 24-month treatment effect downward.

A rough calculation: two of seven offices × 4.1% is about +1.2 points on the control average, applying from month 15 onward. The like-for-like decline is 12.5% to 9.8%, or 2.7 points, so the audit could account for something like a third to a half of it. The exact share depends on how the 24-month estimate weights months 15–24.

So "consistent with some fading of an initial effect" may partly be control offices improving, not treated offices fading. Needed:
- the treated offices' own trajectory over time, not only the DiD;
- a sensitivity analysis excluding the two audit offices (or censoring them at month 15);
- whether the audit was prompted by the trial itself (knowledge of treated offices' practices). That would be spillover rather than coincidence.

## 2. The Summary overstates the decline

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." That compares a timesheet figure with a log-based figure. The like-for-like comparison, given in the body, is 12.5% to 9.8%. That decline is about 22%; the comparison the Summary implies is 32%.

The two intervals also overlap almost entirely (6.9–18.4 vs 4.6–15.2), and the paper reports no test of the difference. "Declined but not disappeared" should therefore be "may have declined somewhat; clearly not disappeared." Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" needs the same qualification.

## 3. The log-in hours measure

- **Baseline.** The log column has no nine-month value, which suggests logs were added later. A difference-in-differences needs pre-period log data. Does the system hold historical logs? If not, how was −11% computed?
- **"Stricter" is not quite right.** Log-in time measures time on the case system. It misses work done off-system (calls, reading, meetings) and includes idle time while logged in. It differs from timesheets rather than being strictly better. Reporting both, as the paper does, is the right approach; the label should change.

## 4. Mediation: the result is good, but "confirms" is too strong

Registering the analysis at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes, is exactly the right response to the post hoc criticism. Some caveats belong in the main text, not only in the Limitations section:
- **Effective sample size.** The treatment was assigned to 14 offices. Office-months are repeated measures, not independent units, so "a larger sample of office-months" adds less than it seems. Was the mediation CI computed with clustering properly handled, using a method robust to 14 clusters?
- **Unmeasured confounding.** The mediators were not randomised. Offices with better managers might both cut meetings more and improve more for other reasons. The Limitations section says this; the Summary's "confirms" ignores it.
- **The shares aren't independent.** Meeting cuts may themselves reduce fatigue. If so, the 47/18 split depends on how the model orders and specifies the two pathways, and the shares are not cleanly additive.
- **Part of the meetings pathway may be an accounting effect.** Treated offices cut about 3.3 hours of meetings per week relative to control, while total hours fell about 4 hours. Most of the hours cut may therefore have come out of meetings rather than casework. That would explain why output per FTE barely moved, and output per hour then rises by construction, because the removed time produced no cases. This is consistent with the authors' interpretation (removing low-value time). It is worth saying explicitly, because it means the meetings share is partly an accounting identity rather than a behavioural mechanism.
- **The denominator.** Does log-in time include meeting time? If not, cutting meetings shifts time *into* the denominator, which affects how the mediator relates to the outcome. Clarify this.

Fatigue at 18% (2 to 34) barely excludes zero. "Contributes, but less" is fine; it shouldn't be read as a firm estimate.

## 5. Per-worker output and cost are still missing for case-processing

Output per FTE is drifting slightly downward (−2.1% to −3.4%, CI now −8.0 to +1.2), with full pay maintained. As in my review of the nine-month report, the county's actual decision variable is cost per case closed: salaries, any overtime, and the per-FTE shortfall. The paper gives a cost estimate for the counter arm (+9% per contact) but not for case-processing. That gap is now the main thing missing for policy.

On the counter figure: with 12% more staff and the per-hour gain only partly offsetting, my rough calculation gives a cost increase nearer 12–13% than 9%. Please show the derivation. Note also that waits worsened from 6.9 minutes at month 9 to 7.3 in months 10–12: service did not adapt over time.

## 6. The Halden subset

- **Selection.** The authors frame the 11 continuing organisations appropriately as "survivors twice over" and an upper bound. Add a third filter: only 14 of the 23 agreed to provide data, and those that declined may differ.
- **The marketing agency.** One reverter was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. The meta-analysis would probably code it as discretionary. So the coverage-bound vs. discretionary split is less clean than "all with client-facing or coverage obligations" implies: deadline-driven client work can bind too.
- **Reverters' output.** Their output indices of 88–91 are a useful bounding figure for the attrition question raised by Varga and Holm.

## 7. Section 5 is mostly fair

- **On "entirely an artifact."** The rebuttal is sound. The Varden 24-month estimate meets the re-analysis's own stated standards, apart from a matter of degree: it is one employer with 7 v 7 offices. One qualification: randomisation does not eliminate a Hawthorne effect from being observed, and the 35% unexplained share could include it. "Not supported" is right; "refuted" would not be.
- **On the meta-analysis's decay claim.** This rebuttal is decisive. It reveals that all four long studies were uncontrolled with scheduled hours. "One controlled study with long follow-up" is still one study, though.
- **Authorship.** The authors include the original Varden team and a Halden author, and the paper is rebutting critiques of their own work. The registered protocols largely address this, but a brief statement of competing interests would help readers.

## Smaller points

- Sick days and resignations still have no CIs, as at nine months.
- Overturn rates at 24 months are now more complete, since more appeals have resolved; state the resolution rate.
- The idea of an arm that reorganises without cutting hours is the right next design, and the authors could recommend it explicitly.

## Where the five documents now leave things

| Question | Current best answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | About 8–10% at two years (controlled, log or timesheet hours); possibly somewhat higher if the control contamination is corrected |
| Durability | Modest decline from nine months, partly confounded by control-office changes; clearly not zero |
| Output per worker | Slightly below control (around −3%), so the hours cut is mostly but not fully offset |
| Coverage-bound work | Fails on service; the randomised arm was stopped |
| Mechanism | Roughly half plausibly from cutting low-value meeting time, though partly an accounting effect; fatigue smaller; a third unexplained |
| Generality | One public employer for the controlled long-run evidence |

The most useful corrections to make before publication:
1. Report the sensitivity analysis on the control-office contamination.
2. Make the Summary's comparison like-for-like.
3. Soften "confirms" for the mediation result.
4. Add cost per case for case-processing.

I can draft a referee report, write the synthesis table up as a short briefing note, or work out the contamination adjustment more precisely given assumptions about timing.
